concepts.name: Reversible reactions
concepts.why: A reversible reaction may proceed in both the forward (left to right) and reverse (right to left) directions, and a special double arrow is used in its equation to emphasize this.
concepts.evidence: Colorless dinitrogen tetroxide decomposes to brown nitrogen dioxide, and nitrogen dioxide combines to form dinitrogen tetroxide, in the sealed tube of Figure 13.2: N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g).

concepts.name: Equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse rates are equal
concepts.why: As a reversible reaction proceeds, the falling reactant concentration slows the forward reaction and the rising product concentration speeds the reverse reaction. When the two rates become equal, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant and the system is at equilibrium.
concepts.evidence: Figure 13.2 plots the concentrations and the two rates, $\text{rate}_{f}=k_{f}[\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}]$ and $\text{rate}_{r}=k_{r}[\text{NO}_{2}]^{2}$, against time until they level off.

concepts.name: Equilibria are dynamic
concepts.why: A reaction at equilibrium has not stopped; it is proceeding in the forward and reverse directions at the same rate. Physical changes such as phase transitions establish such equilibria too, and the concentrations at equilibrium need not be equal, only constant.
concepts.evidence: The two jugglers of Figure 13.3 throw and catch clubs at the same rate, and the sealed tube of Figure 13.4 holds liquid and gaseous bromine vaporizing and condensing at equal rates.

concepts.name: The reaction quotient, $Q$
concepts.why: The reaction quotient is derived directly from the stoichiometry of the balanced equation: product concentrations raised to their coefficients, divided by reactant concentrations raised to theirs. Its value changes as the reaction proceeds, so it serves as an indicator of the reaction’s status.
concepts.evidence: For 2SO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub>, Figure 13.5 shows $Q_{c}$ rising from zero when the reaction starts from reactants and falling from an undefined value when it starts from product.

concepts.name: Writing reaction quotient expressions
concepts.why: From a balanced equation we can write $Q_{c}$ using molar concentrations or, for gases, $Q_{P}$ using partial pressures, including terms only for gaseous and solute species.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.1 writes the concentration-based reaction quotients for the formation of ozone, the synthesis of ammonia and the oxidation of ammonia.

concepts.name: The equilibrium constant and the law of mass action
concepts.why: The constant value of $Q$ exhibited by a system at equilibrium is the equilibrium constant, $K$. At a given temperature it has the same value whichever way the equilibrium is approached, which is the law of mass action.
concepts.evidence: Both scenarios of Figure 13.5 end at the same $K_{c}$, and Example 13.2 evaluates $K_{c}=0.042/0.016^{2}=1.6\times10^{2}$ for the dimerization of NO<sub>2</sub>.

concepts.name: What the magnitude of $K$ tells us
concepts.why: A reaction with a large $K$ reaches equilibrium when most of the reactant has been converted to product, whereas a small $K$ means very little has been converted. The magnitude of $K$ does not indicate how rapidly equilibrium is reached.
concepts.evidence: The text notes that some equilibria are established nearly instantaneously and others so slowly that no change is observed over days or years, whatever their $K$.

concepts.name: Predicting the direction of reaction by comparing $Q$ with $K$
concepts.why: A reaction proceeds in whatever direction is necessary to achieve equilibrium: forward when $Q < K$, in reverse when $Q > K$, and not at all when $Q = K$.
concepts.evidence: Figure 13.6 shows three mixtures of CO, H<sub>2</sub>O, CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> at 800 °C with $K_{c}=0.640$, and Example 13.3 finds $Q_{c}$ = 0.040, 140 and 0.48 for three experiments.

concepts.name: Relating $K_{P}$ and $K_{c}$, $K_{P}=K_{c}(RT)^{\Delta n}$
concepts.why: Since the partial pressure of an ideal gas is $P = MRT$, each pressure in $K_{P}$ is a concentration times $RT$, and the factors collect into $(RT)^{\Delta n}$, where $\Delta n$ is the difference in the molar amounts of product and reactant gases.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.4 finds $K_{P}=K_{c}$ when $\Delta n = 0$, and $K_{P}=3.0\times10^{-5}$ from $K_{c}=0.28$ at 900 °C for CS<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub> ⇌ CH<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>S.

concepts.name: Homogeneous and heterogeneous equilibria
concepts.why: In a homogeneous equilibrium all reactants and products are in the same phase; in a heterogeneous equilibrium they occupy two or more phases. Because the relative concentrations of pure liquids and solids equal 1, they do not appear in $Q$ or $K$.
concepts.evidence: For PbCl2(s) ⇌ Pb2+(aq) + 2Cl−(aq), $K_{c}=[\text{Pb}^{2+}][\text{Cl}^{-}]^{2}$, and water as a solvent is left out of the expressions for HF and NH3 in water.

concepts.name: Equilibrium constants of coupled equilibria
concepts.why: Reversing an equation inverts its $K$, multiplying its coefficients by $x$ raises $K$ to the power $x$, and adding equations multiplies their $K$ values, so the $K$ of a net reaction follows from the $K$ values of the reactions that sum to it.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.5 reverses the ammonia synthesis and triples the formation of HI to find $K_{c}=(2.0)(1.2\times10^{5})=2.4\times10^{5}$ for 2NH<sub>3</sub> + 3I<sub>2</sub> ⇌ N<sub>2</sub> + 6HI at 400 °C.

concepts.name: Le Châtelier’s principle
concepts.why: A change in conditions that affects the forward and reverse rates differently (a stress) leaves the rates unequal, and the system experiences a net reaction in the direction of greater rate (a shift) that re-establishes equilibrium.
concepts.evidence: Changes in concentration and temperature are the two stresses that can shift an equilibrium, since they are what the rate law and the Arrhenius equation say affect rates.

concepts.name: A change in concentration shifts an equilibrium without changing $K$
concepts.why: Adding reactant or removing product makes $Q_{c} < K_{c}$ and the equilibrium shifts right; removing reactant or adding product makes $Q_{c} > K_{c}$ and it shifts left. The new composition differs, but the value of the equilibrium constant is the same after the stress as before.
concepts.evidence: For H<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2HI with $K_{c}=50.0$ at 400 °C, adding H<sub>2</sub> consumes I<sub>2</sub> and produces HI as equilibrium is re-established.

concepts.name: A change in volume shifts a gas equilibrium toward fewer or more moles of gas
concepts.why: Changing the volume changes every partial pressure by the same factor. If the reactant and product gases have equal total molar amounts, $Q_{P}$ is unchanged and there is no shift; otherwise decreasing the volume shifts the equilibrium toward the side with fewer moles of gas.
concepts.evidence: Compressing by a factor of 3 leaves $Q_{P}$ unchanged for H<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2HI but makes $Q_{P}{}'=3Q_{P}>K_{P}$ for 2NO<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2NO + O<sub>2</sub>, which shifts left.

concepts.name: A change in temperature changes $K$
concepts.why: For an elementary reaction $K_{c}=k_{f}/k_{r}$, and the rate constants vary with temperature, so $K$ varies too. Treating heat as a reactant of an endothermic reaction and a product of an exothermic one predicts the shift: heating shifts an endothermic equilibrium right and an exothermic one left.
concepts.evidence: For N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 with ΔH = +57.20 kJ, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right.

concepts.name: A catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant
concepts.why: A catalyst lowers the activation energies of both the forward and the reverse reactions, so both are accelerated and equilibrium is reached more quickly, but without a change in the equilibrium constant.
concepts.evidence: The reaction diagrams of Figure 13.8 show the lowered transition state of the catalyzed path above unchanged reactant and product energies.

concepts.name: Predicting the shift of a stressed equilibrium
concepts.why: Given a stress (a species added or removed, a change in volume or temperature, a catalyst), Le Châtelier’s principle predicts the direction of the shift and how each concentration changes as equilibrium is re-established.
concepts.evidence: The Haber-Bosch process of Figure 13.9 uses high pressures, continual removal of ammonia and a catalyst at 400–500 °C to favor the exothermic formation of NH<sub>3</sub>.

concepts.name: Relating the changes in concentration by the stoichiometry
concepts.why: Whatever the initial composition, the changes in the concentrations of the species in an equilibrium are related by the reaction stoichiometry, so all of them can be written as multiples of one unknown, $x$.
concepts.evidence: For 2NH<sub>3</sub> ⇌ N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>, if [N<sub>2</sub>] increases by $x$, then [H<sub>2</sub>] increases by $3x$ and [NH<sub>3</sub>] decreases by $2x$; Example 13.6 completes the change terms for three reactions.

concepts.name: Calculating an equilibrium constant with an ICE table
concepts.why: Collecting the initial concentrations, their changes and the equilibrium concentrations in an ICE table derives every equilibrium concentration from the data given, and substituting them into the $K$ expression gives the equilibrium constant.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.7 finds $x = 3.39\times10^{-4}$ M from the equilibrium concentration of I<sub>2</sub> and $K_{c}=776$ for I<sub>2</sub> + I<sup>−</sup> ⇌ I<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>.

concepts.name: Calculating a missing equilibrium concentration
concepts.why: When the equilibrium constant and all but one equilibrium concentration are known, the $K$ expression can be rearranged and solved for the missing concentration.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.8 finds [NO] = 3.6 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M in air at 2000 °C from $K_{c}=4.1\times10^{-4}$, [N<sub>2</sub>] = 0.036 M and [O<sub>2</sub>] = 0.0089 M.

concepts.name: Calculating equilibrium concentrations from initial concentrations
concepts.why: Four steps find the equilibrium composition from initial concentrations and $K$: identify the direction of reaction, develop an ICE table, solve for the change (by the quadratic formula where needed, keeping the physically meaningful root), and confirm the result by recalculating $K$.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.9 solves $x^{2}+0.0211x-0.0211=0$ for PCl<sub>5</sub> ⇌ PCl<sub>3</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> starting from 1.00 M PCl<sub>5</sub>, giving $x$ = 0.135 M.

concepts.name: Simplifying the algebra when the change is small
concepts.why: When $K$ is small, the change in concentration may be much less than the initial concentration, so the initial concentration minus $x$ can be approximated by the initial concentration. The result must be checked, and the calculation repeated without the approximation if $x$ is not negligible.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.10 finds $x = 8.6\times10^{-6}$ M for 0.15 M HCN with $K_{c}=4.9\times10^{-10}$, which is indeed much less than 0.15 M.
